paragraphs: A social condition is usually the result of circumstances, sometimes of laws, and more often of the two together. But wherever it exists, it can rightly be seen as the source of almost all the laws, practices, and ideas that govern the conduct of nations. Whatever it does not produce, it modifies. Anyone who wants to understand the legislation and the customs of a nation must therefore begin by studying its social condition.
The Striking Characteristic of the Social Condition of the Anglo-Americans in Its Essential Democracy.

The first emigrants of New England — Their equality — Aristocratic laws introduced in the South — The period of the Revolution — Change in the law of descent — Effects of this change — Democracy carried to its utmost limits in the new States of the West — Equality of education.

Many important observations arise about the social condition of the Anglo-Americans, but one comes before all the others. The social condition of the Americans is eminently democratic. This was its character when the Colonies were founded, and it is more strongly marked today. I stated in the preceding chapter that there was great equality among the emigrants who settled on the shores of New England. The seed of aristocracy was never planted in that part of the Union. The only influence that held there was the influence of intellect. The people were used to revering certain names as emblems of knowledge and virtue. Some of their fellow citizens gained a power over the rest that could truly have been called aristocratic, if it could have been passed down from father to son.

That was the state of things east of the Hudson. Southwest of that river, in the direction of the Floridas, the case was different. In most of the States southwest of the Hudson, some great English proprietors had settled. They brought with them aristocratic principles and the English law of descent. I have explained why it was never possible to establish a powerful aristocracy in America, and those reasons applied with less force southwest of the Hudson. In the South, one man with the help of slaves could cultivate a vast stretch of land, so it was common to find rich landed proprietors. But their influence was not wholly aristocratic as Europeans understand that term, because they had no privileges. And since slaves worked their estates, they had no tenants who depended on them, and so no patronage. Still, the great proprietors south of the Hudson formed a superior class, with ideas and tastes of its own, and it became the center of political action. This kind of aristocracy sympathized with the body of the people and easily took up its passions and interests. But it was too weak and too short-lived to arouse either love or hatred toward itself. This was the class that led the insurrection in the South and supplied the best leaders of the American Revolution.

At the period we are now speaking of, society was shaken to its center. The people, in whose name the struggle had been fought, conceived a desire to exercise the authority they had won. Their democratic tendencies were awakened, and having thrown off the yoke of the mother country, they aspired to independence of every kind. The influence of individuals gradually faded, and custom and law joined together to produce the same result.

But the law of descent was the last step toward equality. I am surprised that ancient and modern jurists have not recognized a greater influence of this law on human affairs. *a It is true that these laws belong to civil affairs. Nevertheless, they ought to be placed at the head of all political institutions, for political laws are only the symbol of a nation’s condition, whereas these laws exercise an incredible influence on its social state. They also operate on society in a sure and uniform way, reaching, as it were, generations not yet born.

a [ By the law of descent I mean all those laws whose principal object is to regulate the distribution of property after its owner’s death. The law of entail is one of these. It certainly prevents the owner from disposing of his possessions before his death, but only so as to keep them whole for the heir. The principal object of the law of entail is therefore to regulate the descent of property after its owner’s death, and its other provisions are only means to that end.]

Through these laws, man gains a kind of superhuman power over the future lot of his fellow creatures. Once the legislator has settled the law of inheritance, he can rest from his labor. The machine, once set in motion, will run for ages and advance toward a given point as if guided by itself. When this law is framed in one way, it unites property and power, draws them together, and vests them in a few hands. Its tendency is clearly aristocratic. On opposite principles, it works still faster, dividing, distributing, and scattering both property and power. Those who despair of stopping its motion are alarmed by the speed of its progress, and they try to obstruct it with difficulties and impediments. They try in vain to counteract its effect by opposing efforts. But the law gradually wears down or destroys every obstacle. By its ceaseless activity, the bulwarks of the influence of wealth are ground down to the fine, shifting sand that is the basis of democracy. When the law of inheritance permits, and still more when it commands, the equal division of a father’s property among all his children, its effects are of two kinds. It is important to distinguish them from each other, although they tend toward the same end.

Under the law of partible inheritance, the death of every proprietor brings about a kind of revolution in property. His possessions pass into other hands, and their very nature also changes, since they are divided into shares that grow smaller with each division. This is the direct and, so to speak, physical effect of the law. It follows that in countries where equal inheritance is established by law, property, and especially landed property, must tend to shrink continually. Yet the effects of such legislation would be noticeable only after some time, if the law were left to work by itself. Suppose a family has two children (and in a country as populous as France the average is no more than three). Sharing the fortune of both parents between them, these children would be no poorer than their father or mother.

But the law of equal division exerts its influence not only on the property itself. It also affects the minds of the heirs and brings their passions into play. These indirect consequences strongly tend to destroy large fortunes, and especially large domains. Among nations whose law of descent rests on the right of primogeniture, landed estates often pass from generation to generation without being divided. As a result, family feeling becomes to some degree bound up with the estate. The family stands for the estate, and the estate for the family. The family’s name, with its origin, glory, power, and virtues, is thus preserved in an imperishable memorial of the past and a sure pledge of the future.

When equal partition of property is established by law, the close connection between family feeling and the preservation of the paternal estate is broken. The property no longer represents the family. Since it must inevitably be divided after one or two generations, it clearly tends to shrink constantly and must in the end be completely scattered. The sons of a great landed proprietor, if there are few of them or if fortune favors them, may indeed hope to be as wealthy as their father, but not to own the same property he did. Their wealth must necessarily be made up of different elements from his.

Now, once you take away the landowner’s interest in preserving his estate, which comes from association, tradition, and family pride, you can be sure that sooner or later he will sell it. There is a strong financial incentive to sell, since money in circulation earns a higher return than real property and is more readily available to satisfy the passions of the moment.

Great landed estates, once divided, never come together again. The small proprietor draws a better return from his land, in proportion to its size, than the large owner does from his, and so of course he sells it at a higher price. *b The calculations of gain that persuade the rich man to sell his domain will therefore work even more strongly to keep him from buying small estates in order to join them into a large one.
b [ I do not mean that the small proprietor cultivates his land better, but he cultivates it with more eagerness and care, so that he makes up for his lack of skill by his labor.]

What is called family pride often rests on an illusion of self-love. A man wishes to perpetuate and immortalize himself, so to speak, in his great-grandchildren. Where the esprit de famille ceases to act, individual selfishness comes into play. When the idea of family becomes vague, indefinite, and uncertain, a man thinks of his present convenience. He provides for the establishment of the next generation, and no more. Either he gives up the idea of perpetuating his family, or at any rate he tries to achieve it by means other than a landed estate. In this way, the law of partible inheritance not only makes it hard for families to keep their ancestral domains whole, but also takes away their inclination to try, and in some measure forces them to cooperate with the law in their own extinction.

The law of equal distribution works in two ways. By acting on things, it acts on persons, and by influencing persons, it affects things. By these means the law succeeds in striking at the root of landed property and quickly scattering both families and fortunes. *c

c [ Land being the most stable kind of property, we find from time to time rich individuals who are willing to make great sacrifices to obtain it, and who gladly give up a considerable part of their income to make sure of the rest. But these are accidental cases. The preference for landed property is no longer found habitually in any class except the poor. The small landowner, who has less information, less imagination, and fewer passions than the great one, is generally occupied with the desire of increasing his estate, and it often happens that through inheritance, marriage, or the chances of trade he is gradually given the means. Thus, to balance the tendency that leads men to divide their estates, there exists another that urges them to add to them. This tendency is enough to prevent estates from being divided ad infinitum, but it is not strong enough to create great territorial possessions, and certainly not to keep them up in the same family.]

We Frenchmen of the nineteenth century, who see every day the political and social changes that the law of partition is bringing about, are certainly in no position to doubt its influence. It is constantly visible in our country, pulling down the walls of our houses and removing the landmarks of our fields. But although it has had great effects in France, much remains for it to do. Our memories, opinions, and habits put powerful obstacles in the way of its progress.

In the United States it has almost finished its work of destruction, and there we can best study its results. The English laws on the transmission of property were abolished in almost all the States at the time of the Revolution. The law of entail was changed so that it no longer interrupts the free circulation of property. *d After the first generation passed away, estates began to be divided into parcels, and as time went on the change became faster and faster. Today, a little more than sixty years later, the face of society has been completely altered. The families of the great landed proprietors have almost all merged into the general mass. In the State of New York, which once had many of them, only two still keep their heads above the stream, and they must soon disappear. The sons of these wealthy citizens have become merchants, lawyers, or physicians. Most of them have sunk into obscurity. The last trace of hereditary ranks and distinctions has been destroyed. The law of partition has brought everyone to one level. [Footnote d: See Appendix, G.]

I do not mean that the United States lacks wealthy individuals. Indeed, I know of no country where the love of money has taken a stronger hold on the hearts of men, or where deeper contempt is expressed for the theory of permanent equality of property. But wealth circulates with inconceivable speed, and experience shows that it is rare to find two successive generations in full enjoyment of it.

This picture, which may perhaps seem exaggerated, still gives a very imperfect idea of what is happening in the new States of the West and Southwest. At the end of the last century, a few bold adventurers began to push into the valleys of the Mississippi, and the mass of the population soon began to move in that direction. Communities never heard of before were seen to rise from the wilderness. States whose names had not existed a few years earlier took their place in the American Union. In the Western settlements we can see democracy at its utmost extreme. These States were founded on the spur of the moment and, so to speak, by chance, and their inhabitants are people of yesterday. They hardly know one another, and even the nearest neighbors do not know each other’s history. In this part of the American continent, therefore, the population has not felt the influence of great names and great wealth, or even that of the natural aristocracy of knowledge and virtue. No one is there to wield the respected power that men willingly give to the memory of a life spent doing good before their eyes. The new States of the West already have inhabitants, but society does not exist among them. *e

e [ This may have been true in 1832, but is not so in 1874, when great cities like Chicago and San Francisco have sprung up in the Western States. But as yet the Western States exert no powerful influence on American society. — Translator’s Note.]

In America it is not only men’s fortunes that are equal. Even their needs share, to some degree, the same uniformity. I do not believe there is any country in the world where, in proportion to the population, there are so few uneducated people and at the same time so few learned ones. Primary instruction is within everyone’s reach, and advanced instruction is hardly within anyone’s. This is not surprising. It is in fact the necessary result of what I have said above. Almost all Americans are comfortably off, and so they can obtain the first elements of human knowledge.

In America, comparatively few people are rich enough to live without a profession. Every profession requires an apprenticeship, which limits the time of instruction to the early years of life. At fifteen they enter upon their calling, and so their education ends at the age when ours begins. Whatever they study afterward is aimed at some specific and profitable goal. They take up a science as a matter of business, and they attend only to the branch of it that has an immediate practical use. In America most of the rich were once poor, and most of those who now enjoy leisure were absorbed in business in their youth. As a result, when they might have had a taste for study, they had no time for it, and when they have time, they no longer have the inclination.

There is therefore no class in America in which a taste for intellectual pleasures is handed down along with hereditary fortune and leisure, and which holds the labors of the intellect in honor. Accordingly, the desire and the capacity to apply oneself to such pursuits are equally lacking.

A middle standard of human knowledge is fixed in America. Everyone comes as near to it as they can, some rising toward it and others sinking toward it. Of course, an immense multitude of people hold the same number of ideas on religion, history, science, political economy, legislation, and government. The gifts of intellect come directly from God, and man cannot prevent their unequal distribution. But because of the state of things I have described here, it happens that although men’s capacities are widely different, as the Creator doubtless intended, they are all subjected to the same method of treatment.

In America, the aristocratic element has been feeble from its birth. If today it is not actually destroyed, it is at any rate so completely disabled that we can hardly assign it any influence on the course of affairs. The democratic principle, on the contrary, has gained so much strength through time, events, and legislation that it has become not only dominant but all-powerful. There is no family or corporate authority, and it is rare to find even the influence of individual character lasting for long.

America, then, shows in her social state a most extraordinary phenomenon. Nowhere else in the world, and in no age of which history has kept the memory, have men been seen on such a level of equality in fortune and intellect, or, in other words, so equal in their strength.
Political Consequences of the Social Condition of the Anglo-Americans

The political consequences of a social condition like this are easy to deduce. It is impossible to believe that equality will not eventually find its way into the political world, as it does everywhere else. It is impossible to imagine men remaining forever unequal on one single point yet equal on all others. In the end they must become equal on all. Now, I know of only two ways of establishing equality in the political world. Either every citizen must be given his rights, or no one must be given any. For nations that have reached the same stage of social existence as the Anglo-Americans, it is therefore very hard to find a middle course between the sovereignty of all and the absolute power of one man. It would be pointless to deny that the social condition I have been describing is equally liable to either of these consequences.

There is, in fact, a manly and lawful passion for equality that makes men wish to see everyone powerful and honored. This passion tends to raise the humble to the rank of the great. But there is also in the human heart a depraved taste for equality, which drives the weak to try to bring the powerful down to their own level and leads men to prefer equality in slavery to inequality in freedom. This is not to say that nations whose social condition is democratic naturally despise liberty. On the contrary, they have an instinctive love of it. But liberty is not the chief and constant object of their desires. Equality is their idol. They make quick, sudden efforts to obtain liberty, and if they miss their aim they resign themselves to the disappointment. But nothing can satisfy them except equality, and rather than lose it they are resolved to perish.

On the other hand, in a State where the citizens are nearly equal, it becomes difficult for them to preserve their independence against the aggressions of power. None of them is strong enough to enter the struggle with any advantage, so nothing but a general combination can protect their liberty. And such a union is not always to be found.
From the same social position, then, nations may arrive at either of two great political results. These results are extremely different from each other, yet both may come from the same cause.

The Anglo-Americans are the first nation that, having been exposed to this formidable alternative, has been fortunate enough to escape the dominion of absolute power. Their circumstances, their origin, their intelligence, and above all their moral feeling have allowed them to establish and maintain the sovereignty of the people.
